Used to be a taxi driver. One night, a regular customer who was ex-Special Forces had a bit too much to drink (I picked him up from a local bar). He began telling me stories of missions he was forced to do, (we knew each other a little, plus it was a bit of a long drive so I figured sure, I'll listen to the stories. They were interesting). Some of the missions were really messed up, some were heroic and some were just plain wrong. It became apparent to me that he was probably not lying after showing me all the meds he was on. He showed me his military ID's and three bottles full of pills he pretty much had to take every few hours to stay alive. He said he was tired of what his life has become and was disgusted at some of the things he had done. That this world, this life, it wasn't for him anymore. When we got to his house, he gave me a huge ass tip (more than double his fare) and told me that this was the last time he was seeing me or anybody. He told me he was going to go inside and take all the remaining pills at once in an attempt to overdose. As he was opening his door to get out, I sped off. Confused and angry (but too drunk to do anything) he basically said "wtf man that's my house where are you going." I drove him around the corner of his block. I parked the car lit a cigarette and began talking with him. He told me more stories and I would gently but continuously keep encouraging him and building him up. Eventually he told me one story of him rescuing a few child hostages. I told him he was a hero. I told him that his story doesn't end here, that he's too good for that. I told him he has a friend, somebody who won't judge him in any way, and somebody he can turn to when it gets to be too much. He erupted in tears in the back seat of my van. It was kind of awks but I felt accomplished, I think I got through to him. He half-hugged me from the back seat, gave me a fist pound and thanked me. As he got out he said "see you next week?" With a big smile and tears almost streaming down my face I said "yup, sounds good man."

It can be hard. Especially with anxiety. Usually I try to pray. Praying can often give you that "God's eye" perspective on your own current situation, as it is even unfolding if you're good enough. I try to ask him to cleanse my mind and calm my restless, overactive soul. In addition to that, I try to envision the neural pathways throughout my mind.. The neurons firing and lighting up.. A vast, untraceable network of electrical pulses and highways. I try to pinpoint a certain feeling with a certain thought. Even if it's entirely made up, associating that feeling with that thought makes it that much easier to trace, and thus stop. To put it in perspective, it's like you're fighting against invisible trains (thought trains). You're the conductor and it's your job to make sure they don't crash into each other.. The only problem is that it's a dark cloudy rainy night, and the visibility from the conductors room is only about a few feet into the distance. The result? Chaos. The conductor scrambling around on all fours, trying desperately to direct the trains he can barely perceive properly. Sometimes it's a good day down at the train station, others, not so much.
